title: Hackathon Networking Matchmaker
short_summary: A networking app for hackathons that matches participants based on complementary interests, previously envisioned with an interactive agent and interest cluster graph. Giacomo suggested implementing it simply using structured fields, embeddings, and profiles in Postgres with an LLM explaining recommendations, though Alex found this approach technically boring. The team also discussed evaluating match quality via post-meeting feedback, though Alex noted it cannot be evaluated in a weekend.
summary: An AI-powered matchmaking tool for hackathon participants that uses conversational prompts to extract rich interest profiles and generate contextual conversation starters. The system relies on organizer registration data, simple embeddings, and Postgres to suggest relevant connections.

competitors.summary: Existing tools rely on passive forums or heavyweight B2B scheduling, leaving a gap for low-friction, skill-balanced team matchmaking at hackathons.

competitors.name: Devpost
competitors.summary: A global hackathon management platform providing project showcases, judging infrastructure, and public participant team-finding discussion boards.
competitors.differentiator: Relies on passive message boards where attendees browse and reach out manually to form project groups.
competitors.idea: Comprehensive hackathon hosting, project submission, and developer portfolio platform.
competitors.shortBio: Devpost is the leading platform for hosting virtual and in-person hackathons, developer showcases, and project submissions.
competitors.howWeDiffer: We actively match complementary teammates using low-friction data intake instead of relying on manual community forum postings.

competitors.name: Brella
competitors.summary: An event networking platform using intent-based AI algorithms to schedule structured one-on-one meetings between attendees.
competitors.differentiator: Focuses on pre-scheduled business development meetings at commercial conferences rather than dynamic project team formation.
competitors.idea: Intent-driven matchmaking platform for corporate event meetings and conferences.
competitors.shortBio: Brella provides AI-driven matchmaking and networking tools to facilitate targeted business connections at conferences.
competitors.howWeDiffer: We specialize in skill-balanced developer team creation instead of executive one-on-one corporate calendar scheduling.

competitors.name: Donut
competitors.summary: A chat-based integration tool that automatically pairs community or team members for casual introductions and social bonding.
competitors.differentiator: Employs randomized or basic lottery pairings inside Slack rather than skill- and role-weighted team composition algorithms.
competitors.idea: Chatbot-driven social introductions and randomized networking for distributed teams.
competitors.shortBio: Donut builds automated social introduction and employee engagement bots for Slack and Microsoft Teams.
competitors.howWeDiffer: We match hackers by technical competencies and project ambitions rather than facilitating random conversational coffee chats.

competitors.market_landscape: Current event networking solutions split between passive forum-based team listings and heavyweight corporate meeting schedulers with burdensome onboarding.
competitors.our_positioning: We position ourselves as a frictionless matchmaking engine that minimizes participant onboarding effort to automatically deliver balanced hackathon teams.

workflow.summary: The Hackathon Networking Matchmaker ingests organizer registration data and participant conversational inputs to build rich interest profiles. It generates simple embeddings stored in Postgres to compute semantic similarity, subsequently producing contextual conversation starters to connect relevant attendees.
steps: Step 1: Ingest organizer registration data and initialize participant records in the Postgres database.
Step 2: Collect participant interests and goals through conversational AI prompts.
Step 3: Generate vector embeddings from the extracted rich interest profiles.
Step 4: Query Postgres using vector similarity search to identify relevant participant connections.
Step 5: Output tailored matchmaking suggestions along with contextual conversation starters.

pros_cons.summary: The team conditionally favors the tool for its practical utility, though concerns linger regarding technical uninventiveness, demo excitement, and pre-formed teams.

pros.point: Mandatory hackathon registration naturally motivates participants to provide personal interest data without extra friction.
pros.source_context: Leonarda noted that attendees are already registering anyway, providing a natural incentive to share information.

pros.point: Conversational agents elicit deeper motivations and problem interests beyond superficial lists of programming languages.
pros.source_context: Marko argued an agent extracts richer context when users do not know how to describe what they want.

pros.point: Using organizer-supplied data, standard embeddings, and Postgres keeps implementation scope realistic for a hackathon.
pros.source_context: Giacomo observed that scoping data to one hackathon and using embeddings makes it a manageable problem.

pros.point: Scanning QR codes to deliver contextual conversation starters offers clear, practical in-person utility.
pros.source_context: Leonarda and Alex endorsed scanning participant QR codes to generate immediate conversation starters.

pros.point: Interest-cluster visualizations can provide an interactive frontend without requiring complex graph database architecture.
pros.source_context: Marko suggested visualizing participants as an interest graph, which Alex noted does not require a graph database.

cons.point: Many hackathon participants arrive with pre-formed teams, drastically shrinking the target market for match recommendations.
cons.source_context: Leonarda acknowledged the critical point that many people arrive at hackathons already having formed teams.

cons.point: Evaluating true match quality and post-meeting satisfaction is unfeasible within a rapid hackathon weekend timeframe.
cons.source_context: Alex pointed out that evaluating whether two people are a good match cannot be done in a weekend.

cons.point: Storing profiles in Postgres with LLM summaries is technically mundane and lacks wow factor for judging.
cons.source_context: Alex criticized the Postgres and LLM recommendation architecture as technically boring for a hackathon project.

cons.point: Presenting text-heavy recommendation lists with generated reasoning lacks compelling visual presentation compared to interactive visual demos.
cons.source_context: Giacomo argued the output risks being an unappealing list of random people with text explanations.

cons.point: Replacing simple registration inputs with conversational prompts overcomplicates the sign-up process for attendees.
cons.source_context: Giacomo questioned the need to replace simple registration forms with conversational agents.

key_risks: Event organizers may restrict sharing participant registration details due to strict privacy regulations.
Conversational AI prompts may generate inaccurate or socially awkward commonalities between participants.
assumptions: Hackathon organizers will readily grant access to comprehensive attendee registration data.
Solo participants prefer algorithmic team matching over spontaneous in-person mingling.
open_questions: What proportion of attendees at typical target hackathons arrive without formed teams?
How can match accuracy and engagement be measured in real time during the event?

systemGraph.summary: Architecture for an AI-powered hackathon networking matchmaker featuring organizer data ingestion, interactive conversational profiling, pgvector-based similarity and complementary matching, dynamic graph visualization, and QR-triggered LLM icebreaker generation.

nodes.label: Participant Web App
nodes.description: Mobile-first PWA providing conversational onboarding chat, interactive 2D interest graph explorer, QR badge scanner, and recommendation feed.

nodes.label: API Gateway & Router
nodes.description: Handles authentication, participant routing, QR code resolution, and coordinates profile chat sessions.

nodes.label: Organizer Data Ingest Worker
nodes.description: Ingests baseline registration rosters and survey CSVs from platforms like Luma, Devpost, or Airtable into staging tables.

nodes.label: Conversational Profiler Service
nodes.description: Orchestrates multi-turn dialogue with participants to extract implicit domain interests, project ideas, and complementary skill needs.

nodes.label: Foundation LLM API
nodes.description: Executes profiling prompt chains, context extraction, text summarization, and pairwise conversation starter generation.

nodes.label: Embedding Generator
nodes.description: Generates dense vector embeddings for extracted participant profiles, thematic interests, and project concepts.

nodes.label: Hybrid Matching Engine
nodes.description: Computes cosine distance via pgvector combined with deterministic heuristic filters (e.g., complementary roles, team status).

nodes.label: Contextual Icebreaker Service
nodes.description: Synthesizes pairwise profile insights to craft contextual conversation prompts when two users match or scan badges.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL + pgvector
nodes.description: Primary datastore maintaining participant profiles, structured registration fields, high-dimensional vector embeddings, and connection history.

nodes.label: Redis Cache & Session Store
nodes.description: Maintains ephemeral chat session states for onboarding conversations and caches precomputed match scores and graph coordinates.

nodes.label: Organizer Registration Data
nodes.description: External attendee data sources (Luma, Typeform, Eventbrite, or CSV dumps).

edges.label: Chat turns, match queries, QR badge scan
Generates adaptive interview questions & extracts summary
Executes ANN vector search and relational filters
Caches calculated clusters and match pairs
QR scan lookup with target user ID
